title: PARCEL NETWORK CONTROL TOWER
description:
One-day delivery depends on time. Each order has to make the warehouse cutoff, get picked and packed, ride an overnight truck or flight, clear a hub sort, and get out for delivery by morning. I built a Streamlit control tower that models this process across a 12-facility US network serving 20 major markets, similar to how carriers like UPS and FedEx plan next-day volume.
What it does
Optimizes fulfillment: a linear program (SciPy/HiGHS) decides, for each order, which stocking facility ships it and whether it goes by ground or next-day air. It minimizes total landed cost within facility capacity and nightly air capacity.
Models delivery time step by step: order cutoffs, pick/pack windows, linehaul speed, hub sorts, time zones, the air hub schedule and out-for-delivery times decide whether each package can arrive on time.
Uses realistic carrier pricing: distance zones 2–8, dimensional weight, fuel surcharge and residential fees.
Finds root causes: each planned miss is labeled as late order, inventory not stocked nearby, or capacity limit.
Predicts delivery risk: a Random Forest model flags packages likely to miss despite an on-time plan, from weather, hub congestion or thin slack. It recommends an action for each: upgrade to air, ship from another facility, or notify the customer.
Runs what-if scenarios: shift order cutoffs, add inventory to a facility, cut capacity, turn off air, or simulate regional weather disruptions.
AI analyst (optional): a Gemini page turns network KPIs into a plain-English operations briefing. Only aggregated metrics are sent to the model, never order-level data.
Results (simulated sample day, 3,000 orders)
Next-day on-time rate improved from 88% to 99% compared with a “ship from nearest warehouse” rule
Removed 165 packages of facility overload
Lower total landed cost including late-delivery penalties
Only about 5% of packages needed air upgrades
